rationale: Drugs differ a lot in how much expression signal they carry: a few targeted agents have strong biomarkers, while many non-oncology drugs are mostly noise. One global alpha=5000 can't suit both. This version picks the ridge penalty separately for each drug using efficient leave-one-out (generalized cross-validation) on the training fold only. It keeps the same multi-output ridge on the top-5,000 variable genes.

A lot of PRISM drug sensitivity depends on lineage, and a heavily penalised ridge (alpha=5000) recovers that lineage effect only partly from expression. This version models lineage explicitly: it estimates each drug's per-lineage mean AUC, shrunk toward the global mean using only observed training values, then fits the same multi-output expression ridge on what is left.

This adds reduced-rank multi-task regression. The 200 drugs' standardized AUCs are projected onto their top-k drug-response components (SVD on the training fold), and k is chosen by grouped inner CV. PRISM responses share a few strong axes (general cytotoxicity, lineage, MOA classes), so throwing away the noisy remaining dimensions should help the many weak-signal drugs borrow strength from related ones. k=200 reproduces the current model exactly, so inner CV can always fall back to it.

This adds a multi-output RBF kernel ridge, a mild nonlinearity that captures similarity between cell lines across the whole transcriptome, such as lineage or differentiation state, which a linear model on genes can miss. It blends that with the current linear ridge. Grouped inner CV on the training fold picks the kernel penalty and blend weight by mean per-drug Pearson. A blend weight of 0 reproduces the current model, so inner CV can fall back to it.

Many PRISM drugs have clear biomarkers in their own target genes (for example EGFR/ERBB2 for kinase inhibitors, BCL2/MCL1 for BH3 mimetics, MDM2 for nutlins). In a single ridge over 5,000 genes, those genes get as much shrinkage as every other gene. This version keeps the same ridge, written in its equivalent per-line form, and adds a per-drug block for the drug's annotated target genes (from `ctx["drugs"].target`) with less shrinkage. Grouped inner CV on the training fold picks one global weight for that block, and a weight of 0 gives back the current model exactly.

Many drug responses depend on genes near the annotated target in the network (pathway partners, downstream effectors, compensating paralogs), not only on the target itself. So I'm extending the kept per-drug, less-penalized target block with each drug's top STRING first-degree neighbours, ranked by summed combined score, as a second block. Grouped inner CV picks its relative weight (0, 0.5 or 1 × the target-block weight); a weight of 0 gives back the current model exactly.

Pathway-level signal (proliferation, EMT, interferon, oxphos, MYC/E2F) drives broad, MOA-wide sensitivity in PRISM, and single-gene ridge measures it noisily. This adds a block built from standardized Hallmark and Reactome gene-set scores (mean z-scored expression) to the shared kernel, on top of the kept gene and per-drug target blocks. Grouped inner CV picks the pathway-block weight together with the target-block weight; a pathway weight of 0 gives back the current model exactly.

At the moment, missing AUCs are filled with the drug's training mean before the ridge is fit. Those made-up values become zero targets once centred, so the fit is pulled toward a flat prediction and the signal from the lines that were actually measured gets diluted, worst for drugs with lower coverage. This change fits each drug's kernel ridge only on the lines where that drug was measured, keeping the same genes, alpha and inner-CV target block. That uses only real data, and drugs with the same missingness pattern are still solved in one batch to save time.

Since round 8, each drug is fit only on its observed lines and gets a less-penalized target-gene block. But the global ridge penalty alpha=5000 is still the fixed value tuned for the old mean-imputed setup, and the right shrinkage is probably different now. This version picks alpha (2000, 5000 or 12000) jointly with the target-block weight by grouped inner CV on the training fold, using one eigendecomposition per kernel so every alpha comes almost for free. The grid includes the current setting, so inner CV can fall back to the current model.

PRISM AUC distributions are often skewed, with a few extremely sensitive lines. In a ridge fit those outlier lines dominate the coefficient direction, which adds variance for the many weak-signal drugs. This round tests a target transformation: each drug's observed training AUCs are also fit after rank-based inverse-normal transformation (rescaled to the drug's own mean and SD), and the raw-target and rank-target predictions are blended. The blend weight (0, 0.5 or 1) is chosen together with the target-block weight by the existing grouped inner CV, and a weight of 0 gives back the current model exactly.

The current kernel weights all 5,000 high-variance genes equally, so drug-irrelevant variable genes (sex, immune or stromal contamination, tissue-specific housekeeping) take up much of the line-similarity signal. This change adds a supervised multi-task gene weighting: each gene is weighted by its mean squared correlation with the 200 drug responses, computed on the training lines only. Genes with shared signal across drugs (for example SLFN11, ABCB1, proliferation and lineage programs) are up-weighted for every drug. A weighted kernel is mixed with the uniform kernel, and grouped inner CV picks the mix (γ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}) together with the existing blend and block weights; γ = 0 gives back the current model exactly.

The kept multi-task gene weighting uses one weight vector for all 200 drugs, but different drug classes depend on different gene programmes (e.g. DNA-damage agents on SLFN11 and proliferation, tubulin binders on ABCB1, kinase inhibitors on lineage and RTK programmes). This change clusters the drugs by their training-response profiles (KMeans, 8 clusters) and weights genes by their mean squared correlation within each drug's own cluster, so each family gets its own line-similarity kernel; small clusters fall back to the global weights. Grouped inner CV chooses between the uniform, global-weighted and cluster-weighted kernels, along with the existing blend and target-block weights, so it can fall back to the current model exactly.

The kept gene weighting uses each gene's mean squared correlation with drug response. Every gene has a noise floor of about 1/n_obs in that score, so the weights are pulled toward uniform and drug-irrelevant genes still take a large share of the kernel. This change adds a sharper weighting, chosen by grouped inner CV: subtract the null floor, clip at 0, then square, so the kernel focuses on genes with real shared signal (for example SLFN11, ABCB1, lineage and RTK programmes), globally or per drug cluster. The existing configurations are unchanged, so inner CV can still fall back to the current model.

Some genes have heavily skewed log-TPM distributions, from dropout zeros or a few amplified or ectopically expressing lines, and those outlier lines dominate the linear kernel. Ranking the drug targets helped in round 10, so this applies the same idea to expression. Each gene is rank-transformed to inverse-normal scores, fitted on the training fold and with test values mapped into the training distribution. Grouped inner CV then chooses between the standardized and rank-transformed gene kernels, each with every existing gene-weighting mode. The target-gene block stays on z-scored raw expression so amplification extremes are kept, and the current model is still in the grid as a fallback.

The current kernels weight genes the same way for every drug in a cluster, so strong single-drug biomarkers (MDM2 or CDKN1A for nutlins, melanocyte genes for BRAF inhibitors, and so on) are diluted by the cluster average. This round adds a per-drug kernel option, picked by grouped inner CV. Each gene is weighted by an equal mix of the drug's own squared correlation with that gene (training lines only) and its cluster weight. The existing configurations stay in the grid, so inner CV can still fall back to the current model.

The kept drug-specific kernel mixes each drug's own gene–response correlations with the average over its KMeans cluster. That cluster split is a hard, coarse partition: drugs near a cluster boundary get the wrong prior, and drugs with no cluster get only the global weights. I'm adding a soft "neighbourhood" prior as a new option. Each drug's prior becomes an average of every other drug's squared gene–response correlations, weighted by (positive response correlation)^4 on the training lines. Close relatives, such as drugs with the same MOA, then dominate, while unrelated drugs contribute almost nothing. Grouped inner CV can choose this or any of the existing configurations, so the current model is still available as a fallback.

Inner CV currently picks a single best combination out of 108 (kernel weighting × raw/rank blend × target-block weight), and many of these score almost the same, so that choice is noisy and gets close to an arbitrary pick. This change averages the predictions of the top-k inner-CV combinations instead, with k ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10, 20} chosen on the same grouped out-of-fold predictions; mixing different gene-weighting priors should lower prediction variance for the many weak-signal drugs, and k = 1 gives back the current model exactly.

Add soft post-hoc smoothing of predictions across similar drugs. Each drug's standardized prediction becomes Z_j + λ·Σ_k S_jk·Z_k, where S_jk is the positive response correlation between drugs, raised to the 4th power, from the training lines. Close relatives (same MOA or pathway) carry largely the same true sensitivity signal with independent assay noise, so pooling their predictions should denoise the many weak-signal drugs. Drugs with no close relatives are left almost unchanged. λ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2} is chosen by the existing grouped inner CV, with S recomputed inside each inner fold, and λ = 0 gives back the current model exactly.

The round-18 drug-similarity smoothing gave the largest gain so far, but the shape of its neighbourhood was fixed at (positive response correlation)^4. That choice decides whether predictions pool only close relatives (same MOA) or also share the broad cytotoxicity and lineage axes across many drugs. This change lets grouped inner CV choose the exponent (1, 2, 4 or 8) together with λ, on a slightly wider λ grid, using the same out-of-fold predictions. Exponent 4 with the old λ values is still in the grid, so inner CV can fall back to the current model.

Round 18 smooths every drug with one global λ, but the right amount of pooling differs by drug. Drugs with a strong biomarker of their own (nutlins, BRAF or EGFR inhibitors) should keep their own prediction, while weak-signal drugs with close relatives should lean mostly on the neighbour average. This change fits a per-drug λ_j = b/a with non-negative least squares (Y_j ≈ a·Z_j + b·(ZS)_j, only 2 parameters on about 250 out-of-fold lines) and shrinks it toward the global λ by ρ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}. ρ is picked by cross-fitting across the inner folds (λ_j is estimated on the other folds), and ρ = 0 gives back the current model exactly.
